steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Intro
  - workload revolves around AI system life cycle, complex multi-stage process
  - build from scratch or use pre-existing models via transfer learning, depending on requirements
  - each approach: own challenges; affects time, resources, technical decisions
### Problem definition and requirements analysis
- either way, start with clear understanding of problem: scope, business context, AI objectives aligned with strategic goals
- consult stakeholders: KPIs, operational requirements
- from scratch: choose suitable algorithms
- pre-trained: evaluate existing models, pick best fit; focus on fine-tuning instead of new architecture
### Data acquisition and preparation
- critical either way; performance depends on high-quality, representative data
- from scratch: comprehensive, diverse datasets; cleansing, normalizing, augmenting; data pipelines; imbalanced datasets, missing values
- pre-existing: task-specific data for fine-tuning; smaller but highly relevant; transfer learning needs fewer data -> faster prep; quality still matters
### Model design and training
- from scratch: design whole architecture; for deep learning: layers, activation functions, optimizers; iterations, hyperparameters; resource-intensive, large datasets
- pre-existing: fine-tuning via transfer learning; smaller task-specific dataset; adjust final layers, hyperparameter tuning; less time/compute since general features already learned
- both: cross-validation, early stopping vs. overfitting; numerous tests to benchmark and improve accuracy
### System integration
- largely same either way; connect model to software components, external systems, databases, user interfaces
- from scratch: extra work to fit operational environment, esp. specific hardware or edge computing
- pre-trained: more flexible, widely adopted frameworks, compatible with modern infrastructure
- containerization tools, consistent environments, cloud or on-premise; ready to scale
### Testing and validation
- from scratch: more exhaustive functional testing; stress tests under operational loads; data types, edge cases
- pre-trained: check fine-tuning adapted model; functional tests for new context
- both: bias assessments, fairness evaluations, security reviews; finance, healthcare, autonomous systems
- explainability: regulated industries, stakeholders needing transparency; understandable to non-technical users; ethical/regulatory standards
### Deployment and monitoring
- same overarching strategies; from scratch may need more fine-tuning in production: memory usage, latency, edge computing
- pre-trained: lighter workload, often already optimized; compatibility with task-specific data and infrastructure
- both: phased rollouts, A/B testing, canary deployments
- monitoring critical: model drift; retraining/recalibration; periodic fine-tuning for pre-trained vs. more extensive updates for from-scratch
- maintenance: model updates, re-validation of fairness and bias checks, security patches vs. adversarial attacks

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The workload of an AI engineer is about the life cycle of the AI system, which is a complex process with many stages. Depending on what the project requires, this can mean building models from scratch, or it can mean using models that already exist through transfer learning. Both approaches have their own challenges and they affect the time, the resources and the technical decisions that are involved.

### Problem definition and requirements analysis

The work begins with clearly understanding the problem, and this is true whether the model is built from scratch or based on a model that already exists. The engineer has to define the scope, understand the business context, and identify the specific AI objectives, which should align with strategic goals. In this stage the engineer also consults with stakeholders to set the key performance indicators (KPIs) and the operational requirements.

If the model is developed from scratch, the engineer also has to decide what algorithms are most suitable for the task. If a pre-trained model is used instead, more of the work goes into evaluating existing models and selecting the one that fits the task best. Using pre-trained models often lets the work focus more on fine-tuning, instead of designing a whole new model architecture.

### Data acquisition and preparation

Data acquisition and preparation are critical stages no matter which development method is chosen, because the performance of any AI system relies heavily on data that is high-quality and representative.

For systems that are built from scratch, the engineers have to gather comprehensive datasets that cover all aspects of the problem domain, and make sure there is enough diversity and representativeness in the data to train the model well. This means cleansing, normalizing and augmenting the data as needed. It is also essential to create data pipelines and deal with issues like imbalanced datasets or missing values, to keep the model's integrity during training.

When pre-existing models are used, the requirements for the dataset are often different. In this case the engineers focus on getting task-specific data that will be used to fine-tune a general model. The overall volume of data can be smaller, but it has to be highly relevant to the specific problem. Pre-existing models, especially ones based on transfer learning, usually need fewer data, and this makes the preparation phase faster, but the quality of the data is still just as important.

### Model design and training

How much work there is in the model design and training phase depends a lot on whether the engineer builds the model from scratch or fine-tunes an existing one.

When a model is created from scratch, AI engineers have to design the whole architecture, and select or develop the algorithms and structures that suit the problem. For deep learning models this could mean designing a neural network with the right number of layers, activation functions and optimizers. Engineers go through several iterations of testing, adjusting hyperparameters and refining the architecture. This process can take a lot of resources, because it needs substantial computational power and a lot of time to train the model on large datasets.

For AI systems that are based on pre-existing models, the focus is more on fine-tuning. With transfer learning engineers can take a model that was already trained on a broad dataset and adapt it to a specific task with a smaller dataset that is specific to the task. This reduces the complexity of the design and training phase dramatically. Engineers don't build the architecture, instead they adjust the final layers and do hyperparameter tuning. It usually takes less time and computational resources than training from scratch, because pre-trained models have already learned general features that only need to be refined for the new task.

Both when building from scratch and when fine-tuning, engineers use optimization techniques like cross-validation and early stopping to prevent overfitting. In both cases training the model involves running numerous tests to benchmark the performance and improve the accuracy.

### System integration
- mostly the same either way: connect model to software components, external systems, databases, user interfaces
- from scratch: extra work to fit custom architecture to operational environment (specific hardware, edge computing)
- pre-trained: more flexible, built on widely adopted frameworks compatible with modern infrastructure
- containerization tools -> consistent environments, cloud-based or on-premise; ready to scale, efficient

### Testing and validation
- from scratch: more exhaustive functional testing of custom components; stress tests under operational loads; domain data types and edge cases
- pre-trained: check fine-tuning adapted the model; functional tests for new context
- both: bias assessments, fairness evaluations, security reviews (finance, healthcare, autonomous systems)
- explainability: regulated industries, stakeholders needing transparency; predictions understandable to non-technical users, ethical/regulatory standards

### Deployment and monitoring
- same overarching strategies; from scratch may need more fine-tuning in production (memory usage, latency, edge computing)
- pre-trained: lighter, often already optimized; compatibility with task-specific data and infrastructure
- both: phased rollouts, A/B testing, canary deployments
- monitoring: model drift; retraining/recalibration; periodic fine-tuning vs. more extensive updates
- maintenance: model updates, re-validating fairness and bias checks, security patches against adversarial attacks

### Model design and training

How much work there is in the model design and training phase depends a lot on whether the engineer builds the model from scratch or fine-tunes an existing one.

When a model is created from scratch, AI engineers have to design the whole architecture, and select or develop the algorithms and structures that suit the problem. For deep learning models this could mean designing a neural network with the right number of layers, activation functions and optimizers. Engineers go through several iterations of testing, adjusting hyperparameters and refining the architecture. This process can take a lot of resources, because it needs substantial computational power and a lot of time to train the model on large datasets.

For AI systems that are based on pre-existing models, the focus is more on fine-tuning. With transfer learning engineers can take a model that was already trained on a broad dataset and adapt it to a specific task with a smaller dataset that is specific to the task. This reduces the complexity of the design and training phase dramatically. Engineers don't build the architecture, instead they adjust the final layers and do hyperparameter tuning. It usually takes less time and computational resources than training from scratch, because pre-trained models have already learned general features that only need to be refined for the new task.

Both when building from scratch and when fine-tuning, engineers use optimization techniques like cross-validation and early stopping to prevent overfitting. In both cases training the model involves running numerous tests to benchmark the performance and improve the accuracy.

### System integration

After the model is trained it has to be integrated into the broader system. This phase is mostly the same no matter how the model was developed. System integration means connecting the AI model to different software components and making sure it can interact with external systems, databases and user interfaces.

For models developed from scratch, integration can need more work to make sure the custom-built architecture fits the operational environment, especially if the AI system is designed for specific hardware or edge computing environments. Pre-trained models are often more flexible for deployment, because they are built with widely adopted frameworks that are compatible with most modern infrastructure.

Engineers use containerization tools to package the model and to create consistent environments for deployment, so that integration is seamless across cloud-based or on-premise systems. Whether they started from scratch or used pre-trained models, in the integration phase they need to make sure that the model is ready to scale and can perform efficiently in the existing infrastructure.

### Testing and validation

Testing and validation are crucial in both approaches, but the depth and nature of the testing can be a bit different. Models built from scratch need more exhaustive functional testing to make sure the custom-built components of the model work as intended. Stress tests are done to evaluate the system under various operational loads, and engineers have to validate that the model can handle the specific data types and edge cases of the domain.

For pre-trained models, testing focuses on making sure that the fine-tuning has adapted the model well enough to the task. Functional tests validate that the outputs of the pre-trained model are accurate for the new context. In both cases bias assessments, fairness evaluations and security reviews are critical to make sure AI practices are ethical and to prevent vulnerabilities, particularly in sensitive applications like finance, healthcare or autonomous systems.

Explainability is also essential in both workflows, especially in regulated industries or with stakeholders who need transparency in how the AI makes decisions. Engineers have to make sure that non-technical users can understand the model's predictions and that they align with ethical and regulatory standards.

### Deployment and monitoring

The deployment stage usually uses the same overall strategies whether the model is built from scratch or based on an existing model. But models built from scratch can need more extensive fine-tuning during deployment so they meet the performance requirements in a production environment. For example, engineers may need to optimize memory usage, reduce latency, or adapt the model for edge computing.

The workload is generally lighter when deploying pre-trained models. These models are often already optimized for production environments, so engineers can focus on making sure they are compatible with the task-specific data and infrastructure. In both cases deployment techniques like phased rollouts, A/B testing or canary deployments are used to minimize risks and make the transition into the live environment smooth.

Monitoring is critical in both approaches though. After the AI system is deployed, engineers set up performance monitoring to detect issues like model drift, which is when the model's accuracy decreases over time as the data patterns change. Continuous monitoring helps to identify when the model needs retraining or recalibration. For pre-trained models periodic fine-tuning may be enough to keep the model performing optimally, while models built from scratch may need more extensive updates, depending on how the system was designed.

Regular maintenance includes updates to the model, re-validating the fairness and bias checks, and security patches to protect against adversarial attacks.

The engineer must define the scope, understand the business context, and identify specific AI objectives that align with strategic goals. This stage includes consulting stakeholders to establish key performance indicators (KPIs) and operational requirements.[1]

When developing a model from scratch, the engineer must also decide which algorithms are best suited to the task.[3] When using a pre-trained model, on the other hand, the workload shifts toward evaluating existing models and selecting the one most aligned with the task. Pre-trained models often allow a more targeted focus on fine-tuning, rather than designing an entirely new model architecture.[4]

### Data acquisition and preparation

Data acquisition and preparation are critical stages regardless of the development method, since the performance of any AI system relies heavily on high-quality, representative data.

For systems built from scratch, engineers must gather comprehensive datasets covering all aspects of the problem domain, with enough diversity and representativeness to train the model effectively. This involves cleansing, normalizing, and augmenting the data as needed. Creating data pipelines and addressing issues such as imbalanced datasets or missing values are also essential for maintaining model integrity during training.[5]

When pre-existing models are used, the dataset requirements often differ. Engineers focus on obtaining task-specific data that will be used to fine-tune a general model. The overall data volume may be smaller, but it must be highly relevant to the specific problem. Pre-existing models, especially those based on transfer learning, typically require fewer data, which speeds up the preparation phase, although data quality remains equally important.[6]

### Model design and training

The workload in the model design and training phase depends significantly on whether the engineer is building the model from scratch or fine-tuning an existing one.

When creating a model from scratch, AI engineers must design the entire architecture, selecting or developing algorithms and structures suited to the problem. For deep learning models, this might involve designing a neural network with the right number of layers, activation functions, and optimizers.[7] Engineers go through several iterations of testing, adjusting hyperparameters, and refining the architecture.[8] This process can be resource-intensive, requiring substantial computational power and significant time to train the model on large datasets.

For AI systems based on pre-existing models, the focus is on fine-tuning. Transfer learning lets engineers take a model already trained on a broad dataset and adapt it to a specific task using a smaller, task-specific dataset, which dramatically reduces the complexity of the design and training phase. Rather than building the architecture, engineers adjust the final layers and perform hyperparameter tuning. The time and computational resources required are typically lower than for training from scratch, since pre-trained models have already learned general features that only need refinement for the new task.[2]

Whether building from scratch or fine-tuning, engineers use optimization techniques such as cross-validation and early stopping to prevent overfitting. In both cases, model training involves running numerous tests to benchmark performance and improve accuracy.[9]

### System integration

Once trained, the model must be integrated into the broader system, a phase that remains largely the same regardless of how the model was developed. System integration involves connecting the AI model to various software components and ensuring it can interact with external systems, databases, and user interfaces.

For models developed from scratch, integration may require additional work to align the custom-built architecture with the operational environment, especially if the AI system is designed for specific hardware or edge computing environments. Pre-trained models, by contrast, are often more flexible to deploy, since they are built using widely adopted frameworks compatible with most modern infrastructure.[10]

Engineers use containerization tools to package the model and create consistent deployment environments, ensuring seamless integration across cloud-based or on-premise systems. Whether starting from scratch or from pre-trained models, the integration phase requires making sure the model is ready to scale and perform efficiently within the existing infrastructure.[11,12]

### Testing and validation

Testing and validation play a crucial role in both approaches, though the depth and nature of testing may differ slightly. Models built from scratch need more exhaustive functional testing to ensure their custom-built components function as intended. Stress tests evaluate the system under various operational loads, and engineers must validate that the model can handle the specific data types and edge cases of the domain.[13]

For pre-trained models, testing focuses on ensuring that fine-tuning has adequately adapted the model to the task, with functional tests validating that the model's outputs are accurate for the new context. In both cases, bias assessments, fairness evaluations, and security reviews are critical to ensure ethical AI practices and prevent vulnerabilities, particularly in sensitive applications such as finance, healthcare, or autonomous systems.[14]

Explainability is also essential in both workflows, especially in regulated industries or with stakeholders who need transparency in AI decision-making. Engineers must ensure that the model's predictions can be understood by non-technical users and align with ethical and regulatory standards.[15]

### Deployment and monitoring

Deployment typically involves the same overarching strategies whether the model is built from scratch or based on an existing model. Models built from scratch, however, may require more extensive fine-tuning during deployment to meet performance requirements in a production environment; engineers might need to optimize memory usage, reduce latency, or adapt the model for edge computing.[16,17,18]

Deploying pre-trained models is generally a lighter workload. Because these models are often already optimized for production environments, engineers can focus on compatibility with the task-specific data and infrastructure. In both cases, techniques such as phased rollouts, A/B testing, or canary deployments are used to minimize risks and ensure a smooth transition into the live environment.[19,20,21]

Monitoring, however, is critical in both approaches. Once the AI system is deployed, engineers set up performance monitoring to detect issues like model drift, where the model's accuracy decreases over time as data patterns change. Continuous monitoring helps identify when the model needs retraining or recalibration. For pre-trained models, periodic fine-tuning may be enough to keep performance optimal, while models built from scratch may require more extensive updates depending on the system's design.[22,23]

Regular maintenance includes model updates, re-validation of fairness and bias checks, and security patches to protect against adversarial attacks.
